dataset_family: Tsukuba speech-app sample (University of Tsukuba Hospital psychiatry outpatients, their spouses and Ibaraki community volunteers; IBM Research Tokyo with University of Tsukuba), Japan, n=114 (43 CN / 46 MCI / 25 AD)
method_family: Self-administered tablet speech tasks; automatic acoustic, prosodic and ASR-derived linguistic features; LASSO feature selection + SVM (RBF), nested leave-one-out CV with permutation test
what_it_shows: A voice app on a consumer iPad Air 2 presents five prerecorded cognitive speech tasks and records with the iPad's internal microphone. The experimenter sits hidden behind a partition. Under nested leave-one-out CV it separates clinically diagnosed MCI (NIA-AA, confirmed by two dementia psychiatrists blind to the speech analysis) from CN with 87.6% accuracy (sensitivity 88.1%, specificity 87.2%). AD vs CN is 91.2%; the three-class accuracy is 78.6%. There is no head-to-head against a specialist instrument.
why: Yamada et al. 2023 (Computer Speech & Language 81:101514). The PDF title, authors and DOI match the map entry. The block content matches the PDF (114 participants; 78.6% / 91.2% / 87.6%), although the block is headed by the PDF filename rather than the title. Against Table A1, every component holds. (1) Consumer-grade: an iPad Air 2 and its internal microphone (p.3). (2) Self-administered: the app plays prerecorded questions while the experimenter stays hidden behind a partition. The experimenter steps in only to repeat an instruction and restart a task the participant cannot follow (p.3). The authors frame the tool as self-administered throughout. (3) Behavioural instrument: cognitive speech tasks (counting backwards, subtraction, phonemic and semantic fluency, Cookie Theft). (4) High standalone MCI-detection accuracy: 87.6% for MCI vs CN (p.8, Table 6 p.10), against a clinical diagnosis rather than a test-score proxy. (5) No head-to-head: the neuropsychological tests only characterise the sample. Caveats the record should carry. 87.6% sits at the bottom edge of ~88-94%. It is the best of six algorithms, all compared on the same outer-loop results (the others reach 49.4-85.4% for MCI vs CN), so it is a best case. The three-class accuracy is 78.6%, and single-task models reach 50.9-60.5%. Data were collected in one quiet lab room, not at home, which the authors list as their first limitation (p.13). One site, one language, n=114, internal validation only. Against the narrowed wording (low-cost data without specialist hardware; best-case ~88-94% in a small internally validated sample; no external validation; no head-to-head) it fits directly. It would be a third independent cohort, so the wording's 'only two cohorts' parenthetical would need rewriting. Independence: authors and site (IBM Research Tokyo / University of Tsukuba) share nothing with P-76/P-77 (Univ. of Denver / MGH-Harvard, I-CONECT) or P-101 (Shanghai Jiao Tong, Memory Guard), and nothing with the other candidates. No other Yamada/Shinkawa/Tsukuba speech paper appears in summaries.md (grep). Side note, not affecting the verdict: the registry row codes Task_Type T3 and Best_Metric 'Acc 78.6' (the three-class figure), so the MCI-vs-CN 87.6% is not in the registry.

quotes.quote: a machine-learning speech classifier using these features achieved 78.6% accuracy for classifying AD, MCI, and CN through nested cross-validation (AD versus CN: 91.2% accuracy; MCI versus CN: 87.6% accuracy). Our results suggest the utility and validity of using a mobile application with automatic speech analysis as a self-administered screening tool for early detection of AD and MCI.
the diagnoses of AD, MCI, and CN were confirmed by two psychiatrists (authors T. A. and K. N.), who are experts in dementia and were blind to the results of the speech data analysis.

The participants sat in front of an iPad Air 2 tablet and answered questions presented by a voice-based application on the tablet in a quiet room with low reverberation (Fig. 1). The experiment was conducted in the same room for all participants. An experimenter sat behind a partition to remain hidden from the participant's view.

We recorded the voice responses in Core Audio Format (44.1 kHz; 16 bits) with the iPad's internal microphone. If a participant could not follow the tablet's instructions, the experimenter gave the instruction again and restarted the task.
We used nested cross-validation with a nested leave-one-out procedure to train classifiers and test their performance.

The binary classification for discriminating AD from CN achieved an accuracy of 91.2% (sensitivity: 87.8%; specificity: 100.0%; F1 score: 93.5%; Fig. 3B and Table 5), while that for discriminating MCI from CN achieved an accuracy of 87.6% (sensitivity: 88.1%; specificity: 87.2%; F1 score: 87.1% and Fig. 3B and Table 6).

The best-performing model was the one using features extracted from the picture description task (60.5% accuracy), followed by the models using features extracted from the semantic verbal fluency task (57.9% accuracy)
